title: An Army General Talks Fusing Sensors and Shooters on the Eastern Flank
gist: The commander of U.S. Army Multi-Domain Command – Europe describes lessons from the Arcane Thunder 26 exercise: soldier-operated high-altitude balloons (Aerostar Lightning) as a persistent layer between drones and satellites, multi-domain company teams that fuse EW, cyber, drones and fires, and data overload as the real bottleneck. He tells defense-tech vendors they are on the wrong side of the cost curve and that attritable Group III drones are the key unmet gap.

themes.theme: Stratospheric balloons as a sensor layer

insights.claim: U.S. Army Multi-Domain Command – Europe demonstrated the full kill chain for high-altitude balloons within its own command during Arcane Thunder 26, launching and piloting more than 20 balloons, including simultaneous launches from dispersed locations.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: The Army is operationalizing stratospheric platforms; an emerging procurement niche for balloon makers and payload suppliers.
insights.locator: The most significant “first” was our ability

insights.claim: The Army deployed Aerostar Lightning high-altitude balloons, designed with the command's direct input after the previous Arcane Thunder, carrying EW, navigation warfare, communications-extension and ISR payloads.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Aerostar is a named incumbent in Army stratospheric ISR/EW; watch for follow-on program-of-record buys.
insights.locator: Specifically, we deployed the new Aerostar Lightning

insights.claim: High-altitude balloons complement the space layer because satellites pass overhead on predictable schedules, while balloons are persistent, maneuverable, cheap and launch-on-demand, giving commanders coverage they own rather than request.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Stratospheric platforms may take some tactical ISR demand from space assets; relevant to the space-ISR vs. near-space debate.
insights.quote: satellites pass overhead on a predictable schedule, while balloons are both persistent and maneuverable
insights.locator: Most importantly, high-altitude balloons augment the space layer

insights.claim: Soldiers, not contractors, handled balloon mission planning, launch, flight control and recovery, which signals a shift of stratospheric operations into organic Army units.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: The revenue model for vendors shifts toward selling hardware and training rather than contractor-operated services.
insights.quote: it was our soldiers, not contractors, who weaponized the stratosphere
insights.locator: Our soldiers in the Multi-Domain Effects Battalion

insights.claim: The Army's multi-domain company team merges drone operators, electronic warfare and space specialists to synchronize kinetic and non-kinetic effects at the smallest units, using balloons, one-way attack drones and missiles to find, fix and finish targets.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Pushes EW and drone demand down to company level, which broadens the addressable market for small EW payloads and loitering munitions.
insights.locator: A traditional combined arms team is built

insights.claim: Training-range policy, especially strict regulation of electromagnetic spectrum use, is the biggest constraint on realistically exercising electronic warfare in peacetime.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Demand for high-fidelity EW simulation and synthetic training environments that sidestep spectrum limits.

insights.claim: Arcane Thunder 26 included the first multinational cyber range integration, with U.S., Dutch and Polish teams running combined offensive and defensive cyber operations in a co-developed virtual environment the command says can be scaled.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Coalition cyber-range infrastructure is set to expand across NATO; an opportunity for cyber training and simulation vendors.
insights.locator: This was the first time our command hosted

insights.claim: The hardest unsolved problem in long-range sensor-to-shooter chains is not moving data but processing and prioritizing the flood of it, so the right shooter gets the right target at the right time.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: The value is shifting from sensors and comms to AI data-fusion and targeting software; bullish for defense AI/data platform vendors.
insights.locator: The hardest problem is the tsunami

insights.claim: The Army wants AI/ML that automatically turns raw signals intelligence into refined target locations and filters out 99 percent of noise, with workflows that keep a warfighter validating targeting data.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Clear requirement for human-in-the-loop AI targeting tools; procurement will favor products with strong validation UX.
insights.locator: An artillery battalion doesn’t need raw signals

insights.claim: Passing targeting data seamlessly from a U.S. sensor to a Polish or Dutch fires system remains a major friction point, although the command can now ingest most NATO platforms and push data to the NATO Mission Partner Network.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Coalition data-standardization and interoperability middleware is a durable spending area on NATO's eastern flank.
insights.locator: A close second is coalition interoperability

insights.claim: Defense tech companies' biggest mistake is ignoring price-to-performance: pitching exquisite multi-million-dollar platforms that cannot survive guaranteed attrition, which leaves the U.S. on the wrong side of the cost curve.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Favors low-cost attritable-systems makers over exquisite-platform incumbents in Army procurement.
insights.quote: If you force an adversary to fire a $2 million interceptor at our $50,000 drone, we win that exchange.
insights.locator: The biggest mistake is ignoring the price-to-performance

insights.claim: The largest capability gap on NATO's eastern flank is attritable, reliable, scalable Group III (medium-range tactical) drones: platforms that meet requirements are too expensive to lose, and cheap ones fail performance requirements.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: A clear market opening for a vendor that hits the Group III cost/performance sweet spot; watch drone start-ups targeting this class.
insights.locator: The biggest challenge I see is a lack

insights.claim: Arcane Thunder produces data-scientist-authored reports with performance data that go directly to Army program executive offices and cross-functional teams as the demand signal for budgets, so vendors that prove capability there gain a path to procurement.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Exercise participation is a leading indicator of Army contract awards; track which vendors appear at Arcane Thunder.
insights.quote: The data is our demand signal

insights.claim: At Arcane Thunder, soldiers and industry engineers fixed a failed drone component within 14 hours and designed, 3D-printed and integrated EW support payloads on several drones in hours instead of the weeks typical of industry processes.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Supports demand for tactical-level additive manufacturing and open, modular payload architectures.

insights.claim: The Army command wants to replace months-to-years requirements cycles with a culture where an engineer in the command post can push a software patch overnight in response to soldier feedback.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Steven P. Carpenter
insights.so_what: Favors software-defined, continuously updated defense products and vendors willing to embed engineers with units.
insights.locator: We want to move beyond reports
